title: 1 Samuel 31:8–13
context: The next day the Philistines find the bodies of Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa, take his armor and head as trophies, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan. The men of Jabesh Gilead, whom Saul had once rescued, travel through the night to recover the bodies, burn them, bury the bones under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fast seven days. Both traditions read this as shared ground on honoring the dead and on the loyalty of those who remembered Saul’s kindness.

verses.text: On the next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines come the next day to strip the slain and find Saul and his three sons on Mount Gilboa. Arminian readers note the bleak scene after the battle.

The narrator keeps the description restrained.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the humiliation Saul feared (v. 4) coming upon his body after death.

The text records the facts without dwelling on them, which models a dignified way of speaking about the dead.

verses.text: They cut off his head, stripped off his armor, and sent into the land of the Philistines all around, to carry the news to the house of their idols and to the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Philistines take Saul’s head and armor and send news to their idols’ temples and their people. Arminian readers note that they treat the victory as a triumph of their gods (cf. Judg 16:23–24).

The text states this briefly; 1 Chronicles 10:10 adds a detail about the temple of Dagon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Philistines crediting their idols, as they had once done with Samson.

The irony is that the God of Israel had humbled Dagon before (1 Sam 5), and he will vindicate his name again.

verses.text: They put his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan.
verses.arminianNotes:
They place his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth and fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan. Arminian readers note the public display meant to shame Israel’s king.

Beth Shan was a city in the Jezreel valley region; the text does not add detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the dishonor done to Saul’s body as part of the tragedy of his end.

2 Samuel 21:12 refers to the bodies in the square of Beth Shan, and interpreters discuss how the two descriptions relate.

verses.text: When the inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
verses.arminianNotes:
The people of Jabesh Gilead hear what the Philistines did to Saul. Arminian readers note that Saul had once rescued Jabesh Gilead from the Ammonites at the start of his reign (1 Sam 11:1–11).

They remember his kindness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see gratitude remembered long after.

The story of Saul’s reign ends where it began, with Jabesh Gilead, showing loyalty to a fallen king.

verses.text: all the valiant men arose, went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth Shan; and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The valiant men travel all night, take down the bodies, bring them to Jabesh, and burn them. Arminian readers note the courage of a dangerous mission into Philistine-held territory.

Burning the bodies was unusual in Israel, and interpreters discuss the reason; 1 Chronicles 10:12 does not mention it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see honor given to the dead at personal risk.

The men’s loyalty contrasts with the Philistines’ contempt. David later blesses them for this kindness (2 Sam 2:4–7).

verses.text: They took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.
verses.arminianNotes:
They bury the bones under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fast seven days. Arminian readers note that “salt cedar” is an alternative rendering for “tamarisk.”

The seven days of fasting express deep mourning (cf. Gen 50:10).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see dignity restored in burial and mourning.

1 Chronicles 10:12 mentions an oak instead, and David later moves the bones to the family tomb (2 Sam 21:12–14). The book ends in grief, awaiting God’s next work.
